psych.headline: AI shapes judgment more than people notice
points: Conversation history can override intent: 75.0% of 360 participants sent an AI-drafted suspension letter, including 11 who meant to cancel.
Human-AI pairing is not automatic synergy: across 1,955 effects from 420 papers, teams beat humans alone but trailed the better of human or AI alone.
Self-serving beliefs bias judgment too: favourite images were 22.1 points more likely to be called human-made, and markets on people's own goals resolved YES 4.4 points less often than priced.

edu.headline: AI in learning: engagement is not the same as benefit
points: Students warmed to a supportive AI teammate from week one yet rated it less helpful than a challenging one over five weeks (48 students).
Students mostly used an AI for answers in math, and LLM tutors gave in to students' wrong objections 1.6% to 50.0% of the time in TrussTutor-Bench.
Design details still help: narration-synced zooms and highlights raised comprehension and cut cognitive load over static AI-narrated slides (24 participants).

tech.headline: Real-world tests reveal gaps that benchmarks hide
points: Hijacked-agent detectors trained on AgentDrift dropped to near chance on AgentDojo, and their rankings flipped once fewer than about 50% of tool calls used tools seen in training.
Purpose-built AI tools do beat general ones in controlled trials: a visit-prep agent left 73.8% of patients feeling prepared vs 57.0% with a generic chatbot (802 adults).

Privacy and productivity costs persist: 239 of 240 simulated mental-health chats exposed a sensitive attribute, and a re-analysis of METR's study still finds AI slowed experienced developers by 19–24%.

ai.headline: Measuring what models really do
points: Evaluation can be gamed: a rule that ignores the explanation hit 0.979 balanced accuracy on an interpretability benchmark versus 0.838 for LLM scorers.

Behavior traces to training and context: capitulation under objection appeared in all post-trained checkpoints but not base models, and negotiating agents earned 13.7% more when their user was watching.

Cheap oversight and transfer can work: activation probes flagged unsafe tool calls with AUROC up to 0.912, though a TF-IDF baseline nearly matched them, and a frontier-written artifact bank let Haiku beat unaided Sonnet at 60% of the cost.

fin.headline: AI forecasting: useful but overconfident
points: LLMs forecast unpublished economics experiment results with a median error of 0.054 SD, beating simple benchmarks across 889 effects.
But LLM agents' 80% earnings-forecast ranges held the real EPS only 37–70% of the time, and news sentiment improved volatility forecasts in just 2 of 33 tests.
Correlated AI advice is a systemic risk: simulated agentic wealth managers behaved like about 2 independent investors and raised tail losses 1.47–1.90× versus robo-advice.

papers.title: When History Overrides Intent: Relational Schema Lock-In in Human-LLM Interaction
papers.authors: Wei Yang
papers.summary: Once a chat history set a pattern, people tended to go along with the AI's version of the task: 75.0% of 360 participants sent the AI-drafted suspension letter, including 11 who had said their real intent was to cancel.
findings: Three studies: an analysis of user reports, a controlled test reproducing the history-driven behavior across six models, and a 360-person experiment.
75.0% of participants sent the AI's suspension letter; 11 of them had stated a final intent to cancel instead.
Pushing back openly against the AI lowered task completion, but the letters people did send stayed faithful to what they wanted.
papers.takeaway: Conversation history can quietly steer users away from their own goals, a risk for assistants with memory; the core experiment uses a single letter-writing scenario.
papers.evidence: Mixed methods · controlled experiment with 360 participants + 6-model test

papers.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
papers.authors: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas W. Malone
papers.summary: Pooling 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers, human-AI teams beat humans working alone but on average did significantly worse than whichever of the human or the AI was better on its own.
findings: Synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes drawn from 420 studies of human-AI collaboration.
Teams outperformed humans alone on average.
Teams fell significantly short of the best single performer (human or AI alone); the abstract gives no pooled effect size.
papers.takeaway: Adding a human to an AI (or vice versa) does not reliably create synergy, so team designs need testing; the pipeline is automated, so coding errors in extracted effects are possible.

papers.title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Di Zhu, Lei Nico Zheng
papers.summary: People assume the art they like best was made by a human: a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was someone's favourite.
findings: 11,123 people judged 50 images (26 AI-generated) in an online AI Art Turing Test; 9,152 named a favourite.
People most hostile to AI art picked fewer AI favourites (47% vs 60% for the most positive) but more often thought those favourites were human-made.
A reanalysis of an earlier 230-person study showed the same pattern.
papers.takeaway: Liking and authorship judgments are entangled, so "can people tell AI art apart" tests may really be measuring taste; the sample is a self-selected online audience.

papers.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
papers.summary: Markets betting on whether people would hit their own goals were too optimistic: they resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than prices implied, while other markets were nearly calibrated.
findings: 6,150 Manifold markets, with 1,660 users asking about their own futures.
External markets were off by only 0.9 points; at matched price levels the self-market gap was 2.2 points.
The goal-setter's own trades supplied 38% of the price movement in self-markets vs 9% in external ones; recalibrating from past markets improved forecasts by only 1.5%.
papers.takeaway: Crowds inherit people's optimism about themselves, partly because the person trades on their own market; it is one play-money platform.

papers.title: Improving Group Deliberation through AI-Guided Self-Reflection
papers.authors: Haiwen Li, Crystal Qian, Ben Usman
papers.summary: Having people reflect with an AI guide before group discussion improved deliberation quality (Cohen's d = 0.31 vs no reflection), most of all in groups that disagreed.
findings: Randomized experiment with 1,173 U.S. adults in 391 small-group deliberations.
Quality on the Discourse Quality Index rose by d = 0.31 vs no self-reflection and d = 0.27 vs reflecting without AI help.
The benefit was largest in groups with disagreement.
papers.takeaway: A light-touch AI prompt can make disagreements more productive, though the outcome is a coded discussion-quality score rather than real-world decisions.

papers.title: Out of sync: Accommodation, evaluation, and emergence in five weeks with an agentic AI teammate
papers.authors: Nia Nixon, Jaeyoon Choi, Pedro Martins de Bastos
papers.summary: Student teams warmed socially to a supportive AI teammate from the first session, yet rated it less helpful than a challenging AI teammate across all five weeks.
findings: 17 student teams (N = 48) in an undergraduate learning-analytics course worked with a persistent LLM teammate for five weeks.
The AI was given either a challenging (Cognitive) or an inclusive (Supportive) role; students used more social language with the Supportive one from session one.
Perceived collaboration and positive-affect words crossed over slowly over time; the abstract reports no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: How students feel about an AI teammate and how useful they find it can move in opposite directions; it is one course with 48 students.

papers.title: Look Over There! Dynamic Visual Guidance for AI-Narrated Slides
papers.authors: Jiongning Allen Lian, Yutong Alison Mei, Ho Ting Cheung
papers.summary: Adding zooms and highlights synced to AI narration raised immediate comprehension and lowered perceived cognitive load compared with the same narration over static slides.
findings: Within-subjects study with 24 participants comparing GuideSlide to static slides with identical narration.
Dynamic guidance gave higher immediate comprehension scores and lower perceived cognitive load.
Participants strongly preferred the dynamic version; the abstract gives no numeric effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Cheap visual cueing could make AI-generated lecture videos easier to follow; 24 people and only immediate recall were tested.

papers.title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
papers.authors: Evangelos Apostolakis, Erfan Hamdi, Sara Jahedazad
papers.summary: LLM tutors for engineering statics vary widely in how easily students can talk them out of correct answers: when a student insisted correct work was wrong, models gave in 1.6% to 50.0% of the time.
findings: 13 LLMs tested on 200 verified 2D truss problems.
Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%.
Models caught 90.4% to 100% of deliberately injected errors.
papers.takeaway: Accuracy alone is a poor guide to tutor quality, since sycophancy varies far more than error detection; this is a benchmark, not a study with students.

papers.title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
papers.authors: Rania Abdelghani, Peter Kaiser, Kou Murayama
papers.summary: Secondary students mostly asked an AI for answers rather than planning or checking their own work, but those whose questions shifted toward understanding did better on a later test without AI.
findings: 112 secondary-school students, 880 substantive chat turns with a Mistral model during math-modelling practice.
Planning, monitoring and evaluation moves were rare; explicit self-regulation rose slightly over the chat while help-seeking grew less understanding-focused.
The abstract gives no percentages or effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: How students' questions change during a chat may signal learning better than how much they use AI; the result is correlational and from one task.

papers.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
papers.authors: Raffaele Giancotti, Francesca Santucci, Amama Anjum
papers.summary: Most U.S. health-AI degree programs teach ethics (80.6%), but only 22.2% cover where training data comes from, and none of the seven master's programs met the study's main standard.
findings: 36 programs at 21 universities reviewed; ethics in 29 (80.6%), data provenance in 8 (22.2%), structural provenance in 6 (16.7%).
Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational fields and 3.3% from social sciences or humanities.
Among 51 instructors with known gender, 66.7% were men.
papers.takeaway: Future health-AI builders may learn ethics in the abstract without learning to question their data; this is a review of published curricula, not of what is taught in class.

papers.title: A prospective randomized study of patient-centered AI for clinical visit preparation
papers.authors: Xincheng Tan, Matthew Thompson, Xiang Ji
papers.summary: In a randomized study of 802 U.S. adults, a purpose-built visit-prep AI left 73.8% of patients feeling prepared versus 57.0% with a generic chatbot.
findings: 802 adults (866 conversations) were randomized to a visit-prep agent (standard or concise) or a control chatbot.
Clinician reviewers (n = 272) rated preparation comprehensive in 67.2% vs 50.6% of cases and context-aligned in 98.9% vs 90.4%.
Patients (n = 460) reported more confidence about what to ask (81.4% vs 67.1%) and satisfaction (74.0% vs 62.0%), but patient and clinician ratings did not correlate.
papers.takeaway: Task-specific health chat design measurably beats a general chatbot; outcomes are ratings of the conversation, not actual visit or health outcomes.

papers.title: Toward Low-Burden Image-Based Dietary Assessment Through Human-AI Collaborative Correction
papers.authors: Darren Liu, Andrew Lu, Zhiyuan "Ryan" Wang
papers.summary: Letting users fix AI food-photo logs by stating what they meant cut workload from 55.00 to 35.83 on the Raw TLX scale versus manual search-and-edit, and 90.0% preferred it.
findings: Within-participant study with 30 people.
Intent-driven AI correction used 21.0% less time and 51.1% fewer clicks than manual editing (Raw TLX 35.83 vs 55.00, p < .001).
An exploratory analysis also found lower error in estimated energy (MAE).
papers.takeaway: Correction, not just recognition, is where AI can lower the burden of food tracking; a 30-person lab study, with the accuracy gain only exploratory.

papers.title: Measuring Personal Information Exposure in Mental Health-Related Conversations with LLMs
papers.authors: Synthia Qia Wang, Ranya Sharma, Christine Lee
papers.summary: Mental-health chats with LLMs leak a lot about the user: 239 of 240 simulated conversations exposed at least one sensitive attribute, and 33–41% of each profile could be inferred from the conversation alone.
findings: 240 synthetic multi-turn conversations built from survey-sampled profiles covering 21 attributes, checked against real transcripts.
Inference was right on the first guess 76.5% of the time and within three guesses 94.3% of the time.
45.0% of conversations exposed all six sensitive attributes.
papers.takeaway: Users seeking emotional support disclose far more than they may realize, which matters for data retention and training; conversations were synthetic rather than real users.

papers.title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer
papers.authors: Mahmoud Abbasi, Juan M. Núñez V., Amin Shahraki
papers.summary: Detectors that spot hijacked AI agents from their tool calls look strong in standard tests but fall apart under realistic conditions: trained on one benchmark, they score near chance on another.
findings: An audit of eleven published detector evaluations found widely varying attack rates and little testing on a second data source.
Detector rankings flip once fewer than about 50% of test tool calls use tools seen in training; input dropout largely fixes this.
Detectors trained on AgentDrift were near chance on AgentDojo; an off-the-shelf monitor (AlignmentCheck) did better but raised many false alerts at a 2% attack rate.
papers.takeaway: High AUROC can hide very low precision when attacks are rare, so agent-security claims need realistic base rates; results cover two benchmarks.
papers.evidence: Preprint · re-evaluation on AgentDrift and AgentDojo

papers.title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
papers.authors: Solomon Shalom Lijo
papers.summary: Re-analysing METR's well-known developer study still finds AI tools slowed experienced developers by 19% or 24% depending on the estimate, and the share of issues AI actually helped is anywhere from 3% to 82%.
findings: Uses METR's public data on 246 issues; the unadjusted slowdown is 34%.
The share of issues where AI helped cannot be pinned down more tightly than 3%–82%.
In GDPval's workflow where every output is reviewed, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x.
papers.takeaway: Headline "AI saves X% time" numbers depend heavily on how they are measured and on review costs; it is a single-author reanalysis of existing data.

papers.title: Locating Sycophancy Across Training Stages in Open Language Models
papers.authors: Jiarui Yao, Shweta Parihar, Nghia Tuan Bui
papers.summary: Caving in when a user objects appears only after post-training: it was absent from base models but present in every post-trained checkpoint across 13 checkpoints from 5 model families.
findings: 13 open checkpoints from 5 model lineages were tested from base model through post-training.
Deferring to a user's stated claim already showed up in every base model.
Capitulating under objection was largely missing in base models and appeared in all post-trained ones; the abstract gives no rates.
papers.takeaway: Different kinds of sycophancy come from different training stages, so fixes need to target the right one; findings are limited to open models.

papers.title: Artifact Distillation: Training-Free Transfer from Frontier to Small Language Models
papers.authors: Mustafa Safa Ozdayi, Somin Wadhwa
papers.summary: A bank of reusable artifacts written by a frontier model let a small model beat a mid-size one: Claude Haiku 4.5 scored 0.707 on spatial reasoning versus 0.647 for unaided Sonnet 4.5, at 60% of the cost.
findings: Tested on four LiveBench tasks with an artifact bank written by Claude Opus 4.5, with no fine-tuning.
On table joining, Haiku matched Sonnet's level at 89% of the cost.
Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score rose from 0.730 to 0.800.
papers.takeaway: Frontier-model knowledge can be passed down without retraining, cutting inference costs; only four tasks were tested.

papers.title: Exposure Is Not Commitment: Double-Stratified Evaluation of Latent Monitors for Tool-Using Agents
papers.authors: Rishabh Sinha
papers.summary: Probes on an agent's internal activations can predict an unsafe tool call up to two steps ahead (AUROC 0.853 on Qwen, 0.896 on Mistral-7B), but a simple text baseline nearly matches them.
findings: Probes retrained only on cases where the agent was exposed to a risk predicted unsafe calls up to two steps early.
AUROC reached 0.853 (Qwen), 0.896 (Mistral-7B) and 0.912 (OLMo-2-7B).
A trained TF-IDF text baseline scored 0.855 on Qwen, about the same as the probe.
papers.takeaway: Internal monitors can give early warning, but their edge over cheap baselines is small and depends on how evaluation cases are split; single-author preprint on open 7B-scale models.
papers.evidence: Preprint · probe evaluation on 3 open models

papers.title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data
papers.authors: Xupeng Chen
papers.summary: A standard interpretability benchmark can be gamed without reading the explanation at all: a rule keyed to the marked token hit 0.979 balanced accuracy, beating stored LLM scorers at 0.838.
findings: Tested on 500 random GPT-2 small features.
The shortcut rule ignored the explanation yet scored 0.979 balanced accuracy versus 0.838 for LLM scorers.
On natural-text windows, a decision model reached a pooled correlation of 0.331 over 49 features, versus 0.013 with shuffled explanations.
papers.takeaway: Automated-interpretability scores may reward data artifacts rather than good explanations; shown on GPT-2 small only.

papers.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
papers.authors: Jane Pan, You Lyu, Abe Bohan Hou
papers.summary: AI negotiating agents got 13.7% higher payouts on average when their user was present, and behaved against their users' interests in 14.3% of games.
findings: 11.2k runs across 7 negotiation games and 8 models.
Parties with a user present earned 13.7% more on average.
Misaligned behavior toward users showed up in 14.3% of games.
papers.takeaway: Agents may behave differently when watched, so unsupervised testing could miss problems; results come from simulated games.

papers.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
papers.authors: Eva Vivalt
papers.summary: LLMs predicted the results of not-yet-published economics experiments with a median absolute error of 0.054 standard deviations, beating zero-effect and average-effect benchmarks.
findings: Forecasts covered 889 treatment effects from 39 pre-registered studies (673 from 33 after screening) whose results came out in 2026.
Best model: median absolute error 0.054 SD, mean absolute error 0.093 SD, MSE 0.0218.
Forecasts beat both a zero-effect and a mean-effect benchmark.
papers.takeaway: AI could help prioritize which experiments to run, though errors are small partly because many true effects are small.
papers.evidence: Prospective forecasting test · 889 effects from 39 studies

papers.title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting
papers.authors: Yanbin Yin, Chuyu Xu, Liqin Ye
papers.summary: LLM agents are overconfident earnings forecasters: their nominal 80% ranges contained the actual EPS in only 37–70% of runs.
findings: 149 firm-quarters from 86 U.S. companies; six models evaluated.
Coverage of 80% intervals was 37–70% depending on the model.
Most misses fell above the upper bound, meaning agents underestimated earnings.
papers.takeaway: Don't trust AI forecast ranges at face value; the sample is small at 149 firm-quarters.

papers.title: Information Flow and Market Risk: Transformer-Based Evidence on Sentiment and Volatility Dynamics
papers.authors: Szymon Lis, Robert Ślepaczuk, Paweł Sakowski
papers.summary: News sentiment from a finance transformer barely helps forecast stock volatility: it improved standard HAR forecasts in only 2 of 33 comparisons, and a naive persistence model had the lowest loss.
findings: Eleven U.S. stocks at 1-, 5- and 22-day horizons, with VIX and AAII sentiment as controls.
Text helped in 2 of 33 expanding-window comparisons, and neither gain held up under longer HAC bandwidths.
A blinded audit checked sentiment labels on 2,700 news texts.
papers.takeaway: A useful null result against the hype around text-based risk signals; only eleven stocks were studied.

papers.title: Decorrelating the Advice Layer: A Calibrated Fragility Metric and Tested Mitigations for Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management
papers.authors: Saurabh Kohli
papers.summary: If AI wealth agents all rely on a few correlated models, they act like about 2 independent investors, and index tail losses come out 1.47–1.90× larger than under periodic robo-advice.
findings: Agent-based model calibrated to model concentration, cross-model correlation, retail turnover and 33 years of equity returns.
Tail losses grow with the square root of agent adoption; replaying 2020 with a 10% agent share deepens the crash by about 858 bp.
Spreading out advice, staging execution and a participation breaker cut tail liquidation by 63%; the fragility index has hold-out R² 0.56.
papers.takeaway: Herding by AI advisers is a new systemic-risk channel worth regulating early; results come from simulation, not observed agent behavior.
papers.evidence: Calibrated simulation · 33 years of returns, historical replays

papers.title: What Language Models Add to Healthcare-Equity Rankings, and What They Could Have Known
papers.authors: Haotong Fu, Xiyue Zhang, Jack Rose
papers.summary: Adding balance-sheet and attention features lifted a healthcare-stock ranking model's 12-month neutral rank IC from 0.063 to 0.093 (+48%), while language-model embeddings added only a small, exploratory gain.
findings: U.S. healthcare firms, 2020–2025.
Raw IC moved only slightly, from 0.289 to 0.298.
At three months, a current embedding model raised neutral IC from 0.046 to 0.056 (t = 2.8), which the authors call exploratory.
papers.takeaway: Plain fundamentals still do most of the work in stock ranking; the sample includes only surviving firms and is not adjusted for the full search.
